A common misperception about mergers is that the companies involved need to be of the same size, resulting in equal ownership. More commonly, the businesses bring significantly different levels of resources to a merger and accordingly the owners do not share equally in the new company. A "fold-in" is a variation of a merger in which a subset of the assets of a smaller company, such as customer accounts, select employees and certain equipment are "folded in" to the larger company and the smaller company ceases to operate. description: Ryan Parshall Business Broker & Former Agency Owner Our Founder, Ryan Parshall grew up in a small town, Odessa, Missouri where he was raised by two determined parents that came from no money. They earned every penny and fought their way into middle-income. His dad, Joe Parshall, borrowed money on a handshake to buy a local grocery store. It’s there that Ryan learned what hard work was all about. ​ His father taught him that good character, honesty, kindness and a servant attitude were the recipes for success. Graduating from Missouri State University in Springfield, Missouri with a BFA in Design, he took his first job in 1993 as an Art Director. He held many key roles that gained him the knowledge and expertise to become a marketing and sales professional. ​ In 2007, Ryan founded Lure Creative, a digital marketing agency in the Kansas City area. At first serving local, well-known Kansas City brands, he grew into HVAC and other home service niches that exploded Lure Creative onto the national scene. ​ After a successful journey in growing a marketing agency, Ryan sold Lure Creative in 2018 and went on to help other business owners as a Growth Coach and Business Broker at Healthy Brands. In 2024, Ryan split the Business Broker part off into its own entity, Exit Mergers & Acquisitions to better serve his clients. ​ Over the years, nothing has changed in Ryan’s recipe for success. Andrew Dibala Vice President Andrew is a Vice President at Black Iron Advisors, where he advises clients and leads all phases of the transaction process. Prior to joining Black Iron Advisors, Andrew served as Vice President at FMI Capital Advisors, an industrials-focused Investment Bank, where he managed sell-side transaction execution across the sector. He also played a pivotal role in business development, fostering key relationships and expanding the firm's opportunity set. Before jumping into the world of investment banking, Andrew served EY as a Senior Analyst in the Turnaround and Restructuring Strategy group, providing advisory services to public, private, and government clients on critical initiatives, including liquidity enhancement, cash-flow forecasting, strategic planning, and comprehensive financial and operational crisis management. In the earlier stages of his career, Andrew worked as an Advisory Consultant at National Planning Holdings and as an Internal Business Consultant at Curian Capital, managing private-wealth relationships and leading strategic sales initiatives. A Colorado native, he has volunteered his time with local non-profit organizations over the years, serving the Leadership Committee for Judi’s House and working behind the scenes as a financial analyst for the Denver Children’s Home. Andrew holds a B.A. in Communication Studies and a Master of Management Practice from Colorado State University. title: Take the   First Step Toward  Selling Your Business
description: Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is a business valuation? A business valuation is a professional assessment of your company’s worth. Our business valuation experts use proven methods to calculate value based on financial performance, assets, market conditions, and growth potential. 2. Why do I need a business valuation? A valuation helps you make informed decisions whether you’re selling your business, planning an exit, raising capital, or exploring mergers and acquisitions. Without an accurate valuation, you risk under pricing your company or missing strategic opportunities. 3. How long does the valuation process take? Typically, the process takes 2–4 weeks, depending on the availability of financial and operational data. Our team of business valuation experts works efficiently to deliver accurate results within a reasonable timeframe. 4. What is needed from me for a business valuation? To provide an accurate and defensible business valuation, our business valuation experts require key information about your company, including: Financial statements, tax returns, and balance sheets Operational data, including employee and inventory details Contracts, intellectual property, or other significant assets Information about your growth plans, exit strategy, or sale objectives Providing complete and up-to-date information ensures our professional business valuation services deliver a report you can trust for selling, exit planning, or strategic decisions. 5. Can I use the valuation report for selling my business? Absolutely. Our business valuation reports are designed to be defensible and credible, helping you negotiate with buyers, investors, or lenders confidently. They are ideal for business valuation for selling a business and business valuation for exit planning. 6. What influences the accuracy of the valuation? title: Preparing Your Business for Sale:  Maximize Value Before You Go to Market
description: Frequently Asked Questions How do I know if now is the right time to sell my business? The best time to sell is usually when your business is performing well, not when you're ready to retire or facing challenges. Strong financial performance, stable operations, and clear growth opportunities often lead to higher valuations. Even if you're planning to sell in two or three years, preparing early gives you more options and greater negotiating power. How much is my business worth? There isn't a universal formula. Buyers evaluate profitability, cash flow, industry conditions, customer concentration, management strength, recurring revenue, growth potential, and operational risks. A professional valuation provides a realistic understanding of what your business could be worth in today's market and what factors may increase its value before a sale. Why should I hire an M&A advisor instead of selling my business on my own? Selling a business involves far more than finding a buyer. An experienced M&A advisor helps position your business, identify qualified buyers, manage confidential marketing, coordinate due diligence, negotiate favourable terms, and keep the transaction moving toward a successful closing. Professional guidance often leads to stronger outcomes than handling the process independently. How long does it typically take to sell a business? Most lower middle-market transactions take between six and twelve months from preparation to closing. The timeline depends on your industry's buyer demand, the quality of your financial records, business complexity, financing, and the due diligence process. Will my employees, customers, or competitors know my business is for sale? Confidentiality is a critical part of every transaction. title: Book a Confidential Valuation Callwith the Horizon M&A Team
description: Frequently Asked Questions Everything You Want to Know Before Booking Is the 30-minute valuation call really free? Yes. The call is completely free with no obligation. We use it to understand your situation and goals. You use it to understand how we work and whether we are the right fit. There is no fee at any stage unless you formally engage us as your advisor, and that decision is always yours. Do I need a specific timeline to sell before booking? No. Many of our best client relationships start 2-3 years before the transaction. The earlier the conversation, the more value we can help you build before going to market. We regularly work with founders who are “thinking about it in the next few years” and help them understand what preparation looks like from where they are today. Is everything I share on the call confidential? Completely. Every conversation with the Horizon M&A Advisors team is treated with strict confidentiality. We do not share your business name, financial details, or any identifying information with buyers, competitors, or third parties - at any stage of our relationship. What information should I have ready before the call? Ideally, have your last 3 years of revenue and EBITDA available - even rough figures. If you do not have those handy, we can still have a productive conversation. We do not need a formal presentation or prepared materials. Just come ready to talk about your business honestly. What happens after the valuation call? Within 24 hours of the call, you will receive a follow-up email from our team summarizing what we discussed and any resources relevant to your situation. If there is a natural fit to work together, we will outline what that engagement looks like. We do not do high-pressure follow-ups.

description: Facility Services: How Contract Renewal Timing Can Make or Break Your Sale Multiple By Dida Goudreau Facility services businesses live and die by their contracts, and buyers know it. When a larger facility services company goes to market, the first thing a serious buyer asks isn’t about revenue or margin. It’s about the contracts behind that revenue: how long they run, when they come up for renewal, and how likely they are to survive a change in ownership. Get the timing wrong and a buyer will price in the risk. Get it right and the same business can command a meaningfully higher multiple. Buyers value a facility services business on the strength of its contracts, not just its revenue. A company with a strong book of business but weak contract terms will get a lower multiple than one with the same revenue and contracts that lock in for years. Renewal timing is one of the biggest levers an owner has, and most owners don’t think about it until an advisor brings it up. The problem shows up most clearly around a renewal that falls during or right after a sale process. A buyer underwriting a facility services acquisition is really underwriting the contracts, because that’s where the cash flow comes from. If a major contract is up for renewal six months after closing, the buyer has to price in the risk that it doesn’t renew, or renews on worse terms. That risk gets reflected in a lower multiple or a structure that shifts more of the payment into an earnout tied to retention. Discounting the price isn’t the only tool a buyer has. title: The Phone Call Every Business Owner Dreads: How to Tell Your Team You’re SellingBy Dida Goudreau
description: The Phone Call Every Business Owner Dreads: How to Tell Your Team You’re Selling By Dida Goudreau I had a seller once who told his foreman about the sale almost as soon as we started the process. He needed information only the foreman had, numbers and history that lived in his head and nowhere else, so there was no way around bringing him in early. Within a couple of weeks, it wasn’t a secret anymore. The foreman had mentioned it to a few people, they’d mentioned it to a few more, and by the time it got back to me it was already a rumor running through the whole shop, distorted in the retelling and completely out of the seller’s hands. Then the buyer, trying to be reassuring, invited the foreman to come see his new desk in their building, months before the deal had even closed. Word of that got around just as fast. That’s the risk nobody thinks about until they’re living it. When word gets out too soon, it rarely comes from the seller. One employee finds out, tells another, and within a day the whole team knows the business is for sale. Most buyers don’t want to fire everyone and start over. They want the business to keep running the way it has been, because that’s what they paid for. But without a clear explanation from the owner, employees are left with whispers instead of facts, and whispers make people assume the worst about their jobs. A different risk shows up when one employee has to know early, usually because that person holds critical information or runs a major piece of revenue alone. If that employee tells a customer or vendor, the conversation can go somewhere the seller never intended. A customer who hears the business is for sale might decide to buy it themselves or decide it’s cheaper to buy a competitor and bring that work in house. Once that idea is out, there’s no pulling it back, and the buyer’s investment is now at risk before the deal even closes. description: Tampa Business Broker Services Tampa Business Broker provides buyer representation to help clients find and purchase the businesses that meet their specifications.  Typically, a buyer hires TBB to do the research and legwork to locate a property that is not advertised for sale but is nevertheless available and fits their needs.  In other cases, a buyer has a specific business acquisition in mind and hires Tampa Business to investigate the possibility of making a deal. As a buyer’s representative, the Tampa Business Broker’s team may also know of “pocket listings” that meet the purchaser’s criteria. A pocket listing is a property that is for sale but has not been advertised via the typical channels. This helps protect sellers who want to keep a sale confidential until an agreement is in hand. title: What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale - Advantage Business Brokers
description: When you’re selling a business, it’s natural to focus on the number you want to receive. But experienced sellers know that a successful transaction involves much more than agreeing on a price. The amount of cash changing hands, the financing structure, the buyer’s ability to operate the business, and the expectations of both parties can all influence whether a deal actually comes together. The key is finding a structure that makes sense for both sides. A buyer may be willing to pay a strong price for a good business, but the amount of cash required upfront can have a significant impact on whether the transaction is workable. Seller financing can sometimes bridge that gap. Rather than requiring the buyer to provide the entire purchase price in cash at closing, a seller may finance a portion of the purchase. This can make the business accessible to a larger pool of qualified buyers while giving the seller the opportunity to receive payments over time. For buyers, the question is often simple: Can this business support the purchase price and provide enough income to make the investment worthwhile? For sellers, there’s a similar question: Can I structure the transaction in a way that gives the buyer a realistic chance to succeed while still achieving my financial goals? The best deal structure considers both. Qualified Buyers Matter Not every person who expresses interest in buying a business is ready or able to complete a transaction. A serious buyer should have a realistic understanding of the financial commitment involved, the responsibilities of ownership, and what it will take to operate the company successfully. This is one reason buyer qualification is such an important part of the selling process. A seller doesn’t simply need someone who likes the business. They need a buyer who has the financial resources, motivation, and ability to move forward. A qualified buyer also gives the seller greater confidence when considering terms such as seller financing. title: Does Your Asking Price Help or Hurt Your Business Sale? - Advantage Business Brokers
description: Seller Articles Does Your Asking Price Help or Hurt Your Business Sale? on September 18, 2026 One of the most important decisions a business owner makes when preparing to sell is determining the right asking price. It is natural to want the highest possible value for a company built through years of hard work, sacrifice, and dedication. However, the market ultimately determines what a business is worth. Setting an asking price based on the company’s financial performance, strengths, and current market conditions is one of the best ways to attract qualified buyers. Some sellers take the approach of starting with a higher asking price and lowering it later if necessary. While this may seem like a reasonable strategy, it can create challenges. Buyers often use the asking price as their first indication of whether a business is a realistic opportunity. If the price does not align with the company’s earnings, assets, and market value, many qualified buyers may never take the time to explore further. An overpriced business can also spend more time on the market, causing buyers to question why it has not sold. A realistic asking price, on the other hand, can create more interest, encourage serious conversations, and lead to stronger negotiations. Determining the right price requires looking beyond what an owner hopes to receive. Buyers evaluate factors such as profitability, revenue trends, customer relationships, growth opportunities, operational systems, and risk. Two businesses in the same industry can have very different values depending on how they perform and how well they are positioned for future success. A business broker can provide valuable perspective throughout this process. Because brokers regularly work with buyers and sellers, they understand market conditions, buyer expectations, and the factors that influence value. They can help analyze the strengths and opportunities of a business while determining an asking price designed to attract the right audience.

While certain industries may experience periods of higher demand than others, buyers rarely make decisions based on industry alone. More often, they focus on the quality of the business itself. A well-managed company with strong financial performance will generally attract more interest than a struggling business in a “hot” industry. Understanding what buyers value can help owners make improvements long before they decide to sell. Buyers Look Beyond the Industry Every buyer has unique goals. Some are looking to expand an existing business, while others want to become business owners for the first time. Investment groups may be searching for companies with strong cash flow, while strategic buyers may value opportunities to grow through acquisition. Despite these different motivations, most buyers evaluate businesses using many of the same criteria. They want confidence that the business can continue to succeed after the ownership transition. Consistent profitability is often at the top of the list. Buyers also appreciate reliable cash flow, accurate financial records, and a business that has demonstrated stable performance over time. These factors help reduce uncertainty and make it easier for buyers and lenders to evaluate the opportunity. title: The Financial Red Flags That Scare Away Business Buyers
description: Selling a business doesn’t require years of perfect financial performance. Buyers understand that businesses have strong years, difficult years, unusual expenses, changing customers, and plenty of other complications. What makes buyers nervous is uncertainty . When something in the financials doesn’t make sense, a buyer is going to ask questions. If the explanation is clear and supported by the records, the issue may be relatively easy to understand. If the answer creates more questions, however, the buyer may start wondering how much confidence they can place in the financial picture they’ve been given. That doesn’t mean every financial red flag will kill a deal. It means owners should understand what buyers are likely to question and be prepared to explain what they’re seeing.

title: The Differences Between Buying a Business and Starting One
description: For many aspiring entrepreneurs, starting a business feels like the obvious path. You come up with an idea, build a product or service, find customers, and grow from there. But starting from scratch isn’t the only way to become a business owner. Buying an existing business has become an increasingly popular option for entrepreneurs who want to skip the earliest stages of building and take over a company that’s already generating revenue. It’s important to note that neither approach is inherently better. They simply involve different opportunities, different challenges, and different kinds of risk. Understanding those differences can help you choose the path that’s right for your goals, experience, and strengths.

title: Is Your Business Sale Aligned with Your Retirement Goals?
description: Have you ever asked yourself whether selling your business will actually provide the financial future you’ve worked so hard to achieve? One of the first conversations we encourage business owners to have during our Strategic Sellability Plan (SSP) process is with their financial advisor. While many owners naturally focus on what their business is worth, the more important question is: How much do you need from the sale to accomplish your retirement and lifestyle goals? Understanding future income needs, investment objectives, tax considerations, and estate planning priorities provides a financial target that helps shape every major exit decision. Without that clarity, owners risk accepting an offer that falls short of their long-term objectives or delaying a sale unnecessarily. The SSP is designed to align a business owner’s personal and financial goals with the market realities of selling a business. As part of the process, we work alongside financial advisors, CPAs, and attorneys to identify value gaps, evaluate transaction structures, and develop a strategy that maximizes both business value and after-tax proceeds. In many cases, the SSP uncovers opportunities to increase enterprise value before going to market or confirms that the owner is already well-positioned to achieve a successful exit. Over the past few years, we’ve worked with owners of great businesses who have done little to no planning with their financial advisor on what they really need for retirement. It’s easy to put a few numbers into a valuation model and get some sort of valuation range, but what really affects overall value and structure is much more complicated,  “it’s not what you get at the closing table but what you keep!” When our firm takes a business to market without a price, offers can range by $1M–$2M for a business under $1M EBITDA, and this range often increases to $5M–$10M or more for a business upwards of $5M EBITDA or more. title: Plethora Businesses Advises Federal Government IT Contracting Firm on Successful Growth Capital Raise
description: Plethora Businesses Advises Federal Government IT Contracting Firm on Successful Growth Capital Raise ORANGE, Calif. – June 15, 2026 – Plethora Businesses, a leading middle-market M&A advisory and corporate finance firm, is pleased to announce that it has successfully assisted a federal government IT contracting firm in securing growth capital to support its expanding enterprise services platform. The client is a specialized provider of digital enterprise IT and cybersecurity solutions serving mission-critical federal agencies, including the U.S. House of Representatives, U.S. Senate, and the White House. The strategic funding will fuel continued innovation, team expansion, and enhanced service delivery across its growing portfolio of government contracts. Plethora’s expertise in corporate finance and growth strategies enabled the client to navigate the capital-raising process efficiently while preserving the founder’s vision and long-term objectives. “We are proud to partner with companies delivering essential technology solutions to our nation’s most critical institutions,” said Bret Schaffer, Senior Investment Banker of Plethora Businesses. “This successful funding underscores our commitment to helping exceptional founder-led businesses access the capital they need to scale responsibly while building long-term value. Our team worked closely with the client to structure a solution aligned with both immediate growth needs and sustainable expansion.” This transaction highlights Plethora Businesses’ expanding capabilities in corporate finance and capital advisory alongside its core sell-side M&A practice. The firm continues to support founder-owned companies in manufacturing, technology, B2B services, logistics, and engineering sectors with tailored strategies for growth, transitions, and exits. Clarity at Every Stage Acquiring a business involves more than identifying the right opportunity—it requires understanding how to evaluate it, how to engage, and how to move forward with confidence. We work with buyers to provide structure and guidance throughout the process, helping ensure that each step is clear, organized, and aligned with your objectives. The Path to Acquisition Engagement is managed to maintain clarity, momentum, and confidentiality at every stage of the journey. How Buyers Engage 1 Inquiry: An inquiry is submitted directly through a listing within the business directory. 2 Coordination: Engagement is reviewed and coordinated by our team. 3 Information: Additional business data is shared as appropriate and vetted. 4 Alignment: Buyer–seller conversations are introduced when there is confirmed alignment. What to Expect While every opportunity is unique, our standard of engagement remains consistent. Structured Process An organized engagement process designed for professional acquisition. Clear Communication Transparency as next steps are coordinated across all involved parties. Phased Access Controlled access to sensitive business data as the engagement matures. Transaction Support Expert support as conversations progress toward a final closing. Who This Is For This process is intended for serious buyers who value a structured, guided approach to business acquisition. title: National Industry Network
description: Business Sellers Sell Your Business with the Right Strategy—and the Right Buyer We work with business owners to navigate successful exits through a structured, confidential process—connecting you with qualified buyers and guiding you every step of the way. A business sale is a significant decision. Whether you’re actively exploring an exit or simply starting to think about what comes next, we help you understand your options and what it would take to move forward. Start a Confidential Conversation We represent owners of established businesses valued at $1 million and above. Our process is designed for companies that have outgrown traditional small-deal brokers and require access to qualified, institutional buyers. At National Industry Network (NIN), confidentiality isn’t just part of the process it’s the foundation of everything we do. When you choose to sell your business, every detail is handled discreetly and securely. Your business information, financial records, and operational data are only shared with pre-qualified buyers under strict confidentiality standards. Our process is built to protect your employees, customers, vendors, and reputation ensuring your business is never broadly exposed. Who We Work With We focus on businesses with meaningful scale, allowing us to connect sellers with buyers who have the capital, experience, and intent to close. While our primary focus is on businesses generating $5 million to $500 million in annual revenue, we selectively work with companies starting at $1M+ where there is strong buyer demand. title: What’s the Difference Between a Merger and Acquisition?
description: Jul 8 2019 Buy-side M&A Sell-side M&A Choosing to buy or sell a business comes with many complex decisions that must be weighed and considered. Critical to making these choices is developing a deep understanding of the options available when finalizing a sale. Two of the most common methods of buying or selling a company are mergers and acquisitions. Both of these strategies are methods by which to combine two companies into one with the goal of increasing the capabilities of both moving forward. It is no wonder that they are often confused and lumped together as being the same, but in reality, there are several important distinctions between them. If you are assessing a merger or acquisition as part of your sale, it is crucial that you know about these differences. What is a Merger? A merger is when two companies join together to form a new entity. This process is typically part of a broader strategy between the two organizations to consolidate resources and produce a new management structure that will help both grow together. Usually, a new name will be given to the merged company, whether a hybrid of the two former names or an entirely new one is the choice of those involved. In an ideal situation, both companies would consider each other to be equal and the power difference between them is inconsequential, which is why a merger is generally understood to be a friendly and planned process. However, that is rarely the case as many leaders find it challenging to agree on all strategic items about how the unified organization should move forward. Such disagreements can lead to a lot of tense conversations throughout the integration process. What Is An Acquisition? In contrast, when an acquisition takes place, a new company does not emerge. Instead, the smaller of the two companies is absorbed into the more substantial one and ceases to exist moving forward. description: Mar 22 2019 Sell-side M&A A few months into 2019, it is easy to start spotting some of the trends we should expect in the trucking industry over the coming year. Overall, growth is expected to slow as compared to what we saw in 2018, which appeared to be a banner year for trucking, particularly in the months after July. Congress is also expected to make spending on infrastructure a priority in 2019. However, it may not be enough to continue to bolstering the trucking and freight industries. So what does this mean for mergers and acquisitions over the coming months? Here’s what we predict and what we’re already seeing for 2019: Slowing Freight Activity According to the Cass Freight Index, the first quarter of 2019 saw the first decline of freight volume in the United States since the trucking recession of 2015. This is likely the result of decreased consumer spending over the past few months. With less freight needing shipment, the industry could begin to contract after a period of strong growth. Decreased Production of Class-8 Trucks In 2018, we also saw a historic surge of Class-8 trucks being purchased by shippers and therefore, their production increased as well. But in February of this year, purchase rates plunged by 58% compared to a year prior. Closely tied to slowing freight activity, the decrease in production of these trucks will continue if freight shipments do not begin to increase over the next few months. title: How to Determine the Value of Your Business
description: Mar 22 2019 Sell-side M&A Whether you are preparing to sell your business or would just like to estimate its current value, it is important to understand how this can be calculated – especially as there are a number of ways you can reach an answer. Of the various methods available, there is no singular “right” way, but there are definitely an infinite number of wrong ways to determine the value of your business – and the value will largely be a factor of the industry in which you operate. And while an accountant or another valuation professional can walk you through your options in detail, you can also utilize one of the methods detailed below in order to calculate a valuation for your company. Book Value Using the asset-based approach, you will simply add up the value of all your assets including buildings, investory, equipment, cash on hand, customer lists, etc. and then subtract any liabilities or debts. You would use this information to then update your company’s balance sheet accordingly and would be left with a singular value. However, this method does not take into account other elements that could make the company more valuable, such as expected revenue and earnings. As a result, this is rarely the best approach for determining the value of a business – though it is one of the simplest and could therefore provide a rough estimate to use as a baseline. After all, if you don’t have a good set of books, your company probably isn’t worth much. Revenue-Based Using this method involves calculating how much your business generates in revenue annually through sales. Once you have this number, you could approach a stockbroker or a business broker who would be able to share more information regarding how much a typical business in your industry might be worth at that level of annual revenue. Some things you might be able to negotiate, such as keeping a seat on the board of directors, but other you might not. So think carefully about what this means to you and if you are prepared to move forward or willing to accept a variety of outcomes. broker_name: joel f. duran, cm&aa, m&ami, cm&ap, cepa, cmsbb
description: Driver 1 Financial Performance The cleanliness, consistency, and growth of your top and bottom line. For buyers Predictable financials drive higher valuation multiples. For you today You know what your business makes and where the money goes. Driver 2 Growth Potential How much more revenue is realistically available with your current systems. For buyers A clear growth runway is worth more than a great current number. For you today You know where to invest next, not just where you have been. Driver 3 The Switzerland Structure Your independence from any one customer, employee, or supplier. For buyers Concentration caps offers. Independence raises them. For you today A single client loss does not threaten the business. Driver 4 The Valuation Teeter-Totter Whether the business generates more cash than it consumes. For buyers Cash-generative businesses earn a premium over cash-hungry ones. For you today You take real distributions instead of constantly feeding the business. Driver 5 Recurring Revenue The portion of revenue you can count on every month or every year. For buyers Recurring revenue earns its own multiple on top of one-time revenue. For you today Cash flow is predictable. Bad months do not sink the business. Driver 6 Monopoly of Control A defensible position in your market, something competitors cannot easily copy. For buyers A defensible niche commands premium pricing and protects future cash flow. For you today You are not constantly competing on price. description: Industry Spotlights Exciting Opportunity: Restaurant For Sale in New Orleans’ Mid-City Table of Contents Duran Advisors is excited to present a remarkable opportunity to purchase a thriving restaurant in the bustling Mid-City area of New Orleans, Louisiana . This vibrant locale is known for its eclectic mix of culture, music, and food, making it the perfect setting for a successful restaurant venture. The current owner is ready to retire, opening the door for a new entrepreneur to step in and make their mark on the local dining scene. With over five years in business, this restaurant has built a loyal customer base that appreciates its diverse and plentiful menu and full bar offering. When the owner decided to retire, they turned to Joel Duran to ensure a seamless transition to a new proprietor. Not being tied to a franchise, the new owner will have the creative freedom to make the business their own, whether they maintain the beloved current offerings or introduce new culinary delights. A Broker with a Focus on Selling As a broker that excels at selling businesses , Joel Duran understands the nuances of matching sellers with qualified buyers. He ensures that sellers receive the most value while buyers acquire a thriving business ready for new growth. Joel’s commitment to the sales process means he works exclusively with clients looking to sell, providing them with expert guidance and support. A Spacious and Inviting Venue The restaurant occupies approximately 3,000 square feet, including a large outdoor patio, providing a total seating capacity of 110. This ample space makes it suitable for hosting a variety of events, from intimate dinners to larger gatherings. The beautiful buildout features a large bar and an exceptional outdoor area, enhancing the dining experience with both indoor and outdoor seating options. The premises are currently leased for $9,500, with two years remaining on the lease and an additional five-year option available. This lease arrangement

This is how Chinook’s process created an efficient and successful sale for a small business owner. Our client approached us to help them sell their business with a common reason: “I’m done.” They had started the business in their 50s and had grown it successfully for over a decade. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. title: Stop being the last step ineveryprocess.
description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. title: Stop being the last step ineveryprocess.
description: COMMON QUESTIONS Your questions, answered directly. If something is unclear after reading through these, the next step is a conversation. We want to understand where your practice is before recommending anything. START A CONVERSATION Do I have to take everything, or can I start with one piece? You start with either the website or the CRM. Deal management is its own software, tied to the CRM, so it arrives with the CRM rather than being a separate starting point. Whichever you begin with is built to connect to the rest, so adding the next piece later is an extension rather than a rebuild. Who designs and builds the website? The Deal Studio design team. It starts with a Brand Sprint to settle your positioning and messaging, then we handle the design, the build, the hosting, and the ongoing updates, and we wire it into your CRM as part of the build rather than afterward. What is a Brand Sprint? A focused working session before design starts. We work through who you serve, what you want to be known for, and how you talk about it, and the site gets built from what comes out of it. Its job is a website that says something specific about you from the day it launches rather than something generic. It is deliberately narrow: the Sprint settles the site, and it does not produce a brand guide. How is that different from a full brand engagement? Depth, and what comes out the other side. The Sprint settles positioning and messaging so the website can launch as something specific to you. A full brand engagement goes further: research into your market and the people you are trying to reach, positioning developed from the ground up, and a brand system built around connected outcomes, where one guide goes on to produce campaigns, content, resources, and new opportunities rather than a single website. description: He sold his own business first. The deal that started it. The story, in full: Scot had built a successful business many years before — a janitorial company cleaning high-rise buildings at night, with a large number of employees. Then he purchased another business that did make-readys for apartments and rental properties. He bought it for their commercial contracts. But after he acquired it, he discovered something the previous owner had missed: there was a highly profitable, massively underserved market in the make-ready side of the business. Once he saw it, he scaled into it aggressively. The business grew dramatically. Government regulations and a weak labor market — he was scaling faster than he could hire — made him decide to sell. That’s when he started looking for a broker. It was 2003. You found brokers in the newspaper and phone book. He called four brokers. Some didn’t call back. Some he met in person. One came to his office and walked him through exactly how they sold businesses. But he never asked Scot any questions. Didn’t ask about the business. Didn’t ask what he wanted to sell it for. Didn’t try to understand the owner or what he’d built. He just talked about himself and his process. Scot realized something that day: if he’s only interested in himself, he’s going to stay interested in himself when he lists my business. He needed a broker who was interested in him. He chose a different broker — one who claimed they’d sold more businesses than anyone in America. It sounded credible. It turned out later to be a trademark with no basis in reality. title: 1143 VERNON RD, HARRINGTON, DE, 19952
description:
BE YOUR OWN BOSS - Welcome to Chicky-Juana. If you have ever wanted to grow chickens and have a full 1/2 acre of programmable automatic greenhouse with rolling tables - STOP You are not HIGH and such a fantasy place exists.  
This beautiful 21.9 acre chicken farm has two 43' X 550' clear span houses with updated fan motors, feed lines, drink lines, tunnel doors, solid meatal sides, LED lights, exhaust fans, stir fans and even includes some farm equipment. Both greenhouse and chicken houses are fully functional. Flock reports are available upon request.  
The 2-story home has 4 bedrooms, with a first floor primary, 3 full baths, water purification, pellet stove, dual AC and they will even leave the above ground pool. The home has been beautifully maintained and is ready for it's new owners.  
There is even an additional 5 acres of tillable land and the pond is filled with fish. Hunting is abundant and deer are all around. You can be self sufficient. Several buildings can easily be outfitted for horses or live stock. This is a dream setting for the family that wants to live on the land.

title: 692 BAYVIEW ROAD, MIDDLETOWN, DE, 19709
description:
A lovely brick federal style home with some Georgian characteristics. This home is placed on the national historic register. The property itself is 14.6 acres improved by mature trees, magnificent boxwoods, and lots of privacy. The home and numerous outbuildings were originally built during the local peach era, making Monterey one of Middletown's peach plantation homes. The outbuildings have just as much history as the main house.  
Additionally featured are several barns, a second 3 bedroom home, 4 car garage, and a 3 hole privy which is also on the historic register along with the unique ice and smoke houses.  
This country estate home is a great opportunity to add your restoration touches and make this your farmette in which to raise your kids, horses, and animals. 
No homesale contingencies

title: 30402 JAY PATCH ROAD, SELBYVILLE, DE, 19975
description: Welcome to the only USDA certified organic farm in Sussex County!  This 5.69 acre farm has everything you need to start farming this Spring 2026 including relationships with 4 local Farmers Markets and local restaurants.  DBA as Herb Spice Everything Nice for the past 20 years, the name is a well-known business in the Sussex County produce community.  The farm includes 2 greenhouses, 5 high tunnels, a 36 x 48 pole barn with an attached front porch and an attached 8 x 12 Vegetable Cooler/Propagation with 230 and 110 volt electric.  The field areas are protected with a 7.5 ft deer fence.  Included equipment is a 2008 Cub Cadet Tractor with a front load bucket and only 975 hours of use.  Compatible with the tractor includes a 60 inch tiller, 6 ft rear mower and a 30 inch bed layer with drip irrigation attachment.  See the Addendum for the full list of included equipment.  A 2016 Transit 250 truck fitted with shelving for produce delivery is negotiable.

title: 13651 WILSON HILL ROAD, GEORGETOWN, DE, 19947
description:
Three-house poultry farm in a strong Sussex County location with frontage on both Route 18 and Wilson Hill Road. Currently growing for Perdue, this property offers a solid opportunity for a buyer seeking existing poultry income, cropland value, and upside through approved improvements.

The poultry houses include a 44' x 460' house built in 1964, a 40' x 440' house built in 1974, and a 40' x 400' house built in 1984. House #2 recently experienced a fire and will require all new equipment, though the structure itself was not damaged. A replacement equipment quote from Marydel Ag is available at approximately $198,000. The farm is equipped with Chore-Time Model 40 controllers, Cyclone feeders in House #1, Chore-Time feeders in House #3, new nipples in both active houses, 3-year-old box heaters, three wells, and a 105 kW John Deere generator with approximately 1,200 hours. Electric service is provided by Delaware Electric Co-op.

Seller has already completed Perdue’s recent requirement for seven box heaters per house and $40,000 in foundation repairs on Houses 1 and 3. In addition, the farm has been approved through Energize Delaware for new doors, metal, plywood, and insulation to create solid side walls, plus ceiling re-insulation. The total quote is approximately $170,000, with 80% covered by Energize Delaware and the balance eligible for 3% financing. Seller is moving forward with the improvements but may also transfer the benefit of the approval to Buyer.

Nearly all remaining land is cleared tillable cropland, and the property offers highly favorable soils for a potential residential septic system, subject to Buyer’s own due diligence.

No showings inside the chicken houses unless birds are out.

Website, search marketing, social media, content, and PR all work together to create a robust experience for potential clients. Just like any highrise, the foundation is the most important piece for longevity. DO I NEED A MARKETING AGENCY THAT SPECIALIZES IN COMMERCIAL REAL ESTATE? While some marketing agencies specialize in commercial real estate, it’s not necessary to hire an agency that works exclusively with CRE firms. Often, it’s even better to work with an agency that has a wide range of industry experience. While the general agency may not be in the know of the nitty-gritty details of the industry, they are well-tuned to the algorithms that run search engines and social media. Knowing the digital landscape is far more important than understanding the commercial market trends when it comes to gaining brand visibility & leads. DO REAL ESTATE BROKERS NEED THEIR OWN DIGITAL MARKETING STRATEGY Brokers who have an intricate understanding of digital marketing far outperform those who solely rely on networking and personal connections. However, it’s vital to coordinate overall brand strategy with individual brokers to align on messaging and ideal clients that lead to revenue. title: What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale
description: Seller Articles What Buyers Really Want From a Business Sale September 25, 2026 When you’re selling a business, it’s natural to focus on the number you want to receive. But experienced sellers know that a successful transaction involves much more than agreeing on a price. The amount of cash changing hands, the financing structure, the buyer’s ability to operate the business, and the expectations of both parties can all influence whether a deal actually comes together. The key is finding a structure that makes sense for both sides. A buyer may be willing to pay a strong price for a good business, but the amount of cash required upfront can have a significant impact on whether the transaction is workable. Seller financing can sometimes bridge that gap. Rather than requiring the buyer to provide the entire purchase price in cash at closing, a seller may finance a portion of the purchase. This can make the business accessible to a larger pool of qualified buyers while giving the seller the opportunity to receive payments over time. For buyers, the question is often simple: Can this business support the purchase price and provide enough income to make the investment worthwhile? For sellers, there’s a similar question: Can I structure the transaction in a way that gives the buyer a realistic chance to succeed while still achieving my financial goals? The best deal structure considers both. Qualified Buyers Matter Not every person who expresses interest in buying a business is ready or able to complete a transaction. A serious buyer should have a realistic understanding of the financial commitment involved, the responsibilities of ownership, and what it will take to operate the company successfully.
